question: The elevator, ailerons and rudder control rotation about, respectively:

options.text: The lateral, longitudinal and normal axes
The lateral, normal and longitudinal axes
The longitudinal, lateral and normal axes
The normal, longitudinal and lateral axes

explanation: Pitch is rotation about the lateral axis, roll about the longitudinal axis, yaw about the normal axis; all three pass through the CG.

question: A control surface deflection changes the force on its lifting surface mainly by:

options.text: Changing the section camber and zero-lift angle

explanation: Deflection adds camber: ΔCL = a·τ·δ, with τ the flap-effectiveness factor set by control-chord ratio.

question: Tail: S_t = 20 m², arm 15 m, q = 6 kPa. An elevator deflection changes the tail CL by 0.1. The pitching-moment change about the CG is:
Control power (moment per unit deflection) at constant configuration is proportional to:

options.text: The square root of dynamic pressure

explanation: Moment = ΔC·q·S·l. At 0.7 of a reference EAS, control power is 0.49 of the reference value — the reason controls feel sluggish at low speed.

question: Tail volume coefficient V_H = S_t·l_t/(S·c̄). With S_t = 20 m², l_t = 15 m, S = 120 m², c̄ = 3.7 m, V_H is:
explanation: V_H = 300/444 = 0.68. It measures the tail's pitch authority and stabilising power relative to the wing.

question: Hinge moment H = C_h·q·S_c·c_c. With C_h = −0.005 per degree, δ = 10°, q = 5 kPa, S_c = 2 m², c_c = 0.4 m, |H| is:
With a stick gearing of 1.5 rad/m, a hinge moment of 200 N·m requires a stick force of:
explanation: F = G·H = 1.5 × 200 = 300 N (work balance: F·ds = H·dδ).

question: At constant deflection, speed increases by 50 %. The hinge moment and stick force change by:
The hinge moment coefficient C_h = b₁·α + b₂·δ. Aerodynamic balance aims to:

options.text: Make C_h independent of δ by making it infinite
Reduce the magnitude of b₂ (and b₁) so that less force is needed
Reverse the sign of the lift

explanation: b₂ sets force per deflection; b₁ sets the floating tendency. Balancing reduces both while keeping the sign that gives natural centring.

question: A free (released) elevator tends to float in the direction of the local flow because:

options.text: The CG of the elevator is ahead of the hinge
The angle-of-attack term b₁·α produces a hinge moment that trails the surface

explanation: With the stick released, H = 0 → δ_float = −(b₁/b₂)·α. The floating elevator reduces tail effectiveness — the stick-free stability reduction.

question: With manual reversible controls at very high q, the pilot may be unable to achieve full deflection because:

options.text: The hinge moment exceeds the available pilot force (control blow-back)

explanation: H ∝ q; at high speed the achievable deflection is limited by pilot strength, and in powered systems by actuator stall load.

question: A horn balance reduces hinge moment by:

options.text: Moving the hinge aft of the surface
Placing part of the surface area ahead of the hinge line, where its lift opposes the main surface's moment
Adding weight ahead of the hinge

explanation: Air load on the horn acts ahead of the hinge, producing a moment of opposite sign to that of the area behind it.

question: An inset (set-back) hinge reduces hinge moment because:

options.text: The hinge moves aft toward the centre of pressure of the surface load, shortening the moment arm
It moves the surface CG forward only

explanation: H = load × distance from hinge to its centre of pressure. Setting the hinge back reduces that distance.

question: An internal (sealed) balance works by:

options.text: The pressure difference across a balance panel ahead of the hinge, inside the wing, opposing the hinge moment

explanation: The seal separates the upper and lower pressures in a cavity; the panel, hinged ahead of the surface, feels a load that opposes the main moment.

question: Excessive aerodynamic balance (overbalance) produces:

options.text: Hinge-moment reversal, so the surface tends to run to full deflection

explanation: If the balancing moment exceeds the main one, C_h changes sign: the pilot must hold the surface back from full travel — unacceptable.

question: A balance tab deflects:

options.text: Opposite to the control surface, reducing the hinge moment
In the same direction as the surface, increasing force

explanation: Linkage moves the tab against the surface; the tab's lift produces a moment about the hinge that assists the pilot.

question: An anti-balance tab on an all-moving tailplane:

options.text: Is used only at low speed
Deflects in the same direction as the surface, increasing stick force to prevent over-controlling

explanation: A stabilator's hinge moments are small (pivot near its aerodynamic centre); the anti-balance tab adds feel and increases stability of the control.

question: With a servo tab, the pilot's controls move:

options.text: The surface directly, with the tab following
The tab only; the tab's aerodynamic force deflects the free-floating control surface
Both surface and tab rigidly together

explanation: Tab deflects one way, surface goes the other. Force is low, but at very low speed (taxi, early take-off roll) control is weak.

question: A spring tab provides:

options.text: Direct control at low speed and increasing tab assistance as hinge moments grow with speed

explanation: The pilot's input goes through a spring. At low q the spring barely deflects (direct drive); at high q the hinge moment compresses it and the tab deflects to help.

question: Mass balancing a control surface places its centre of gravity:

options.text: Aft of the hinge line to increase feel
On or ahead of the hinge line, to prevent flutter
At the tip of the horn only for aerodynamic balance

explanation: An aft CG couples surface rotation with wing or tail bending through inertia; putting mass ahead of the hinge removes that coupling.

question: Flutter is:

options.text: A self-excited oscillation from coupling of aerodynamic forces with structural bending and torsion, growing above a critical speed

explanation: Above the flutter speed aerodynamic energy input exceeds structural damping; amplitude grows rapidly to failure. Stiffness, mass distribution and mass balance set that speed.

question: Ice or water accumulation behind a control surface hinge, or loose control cables, can:

options.text: Remove the need for mass balance

explanation: Added mass aft of the hinge and freeplay reduce effective mass balance and stiffness.

question: Steady roll rate for a given aileron deflection is set by pb/2V ≈ constant. With pb/2V = 0.07, b = 30 m, V = 100 m/s, the roll rate is:
For the same aileron deflection (rigid wing), increasing TAS from 100 to 150 m/s changes the steady roll rate from 27°/s to:
explanation: Driving and damping moments both scale with q, so pb/2V is constant and p ∝ V: 26.7 × 1.5 = 40°/s.

question: A roll rate of 0.5 rad/s at 100 m/s changes the local angle of attack at 15 m span station by:
explanation: Δα = p·y/V = 0.5 × 15/100 = 0.075 rad = 4.3°: up on the descending wing, down on the rising wing — roll damping.

question: Roll damping arises because:

options.text: The down-going wing sees increased α and lift, the up-going wing decreased α and lift
The fin produces a rolling moment
Induced drag is zero in roll

explanation: The roll-induced α distribution produces a moment opposing the roll rate, so a fixed aileron deflection gives a steady rate, not a steady acceleration.

question: Fuel in the outer wing increases roll inertia. This mainly affects:

options.text: Roll acceleration (time to reach steady rate), not the steady roll rate

explanation: Steady rate is set by aerodynamic balance of control and damping moments; inertia governs how quickly it is reached.

question: At the same EAS and aileron deflection, the steady roll rate at altitude compared with sea level is:
explanation: pb/2V is independent of density (both moments ∝ q); p ∝ V_T = V_E/√σ.

question: To roll right, the aileron positions are:

options.text: Right aileron up, left aileron down
Right aileron down, left aileron up

explanation: The left wing's increased camber raises its lift; the right wing's reduced camber lowers its lift.

question: Roll spoilers (upper-surface panels raised on the down-going wing):

options.text: Reduce lift and add drag on that wing, giving proverse yaw

explanation: Spoiling lift on the descending wing rolls the aircraft; its extra drag yaws the nose into the turn, the opposite of aileron adverse yaw.

question: Near the stall, large aileron deflection is undesirable mainly because:

options.text: Ailerons are ineffective above the stall only on swept wings
The down-going aileron raises local α and can stall the wing it is meant to lift

explanation: Down-aileron increases local camber; a wing near α_crit separates, losing lift and adding drag — roll reversal and yaw toward the low wing.

question: Adverse yaw from aileron deflection is caused by:

options.text: Lower drag on the rising wing
Higher induced and profile drag on the wing with the down-going aileron (the up-going wing)

explanation: The rising wing produces more lift, hence more induced drag, and the down-aileron adds profile drag: the nose yaws away from the intended turn.

question: Adverse yaw is greatest:

options.text: At low speed and high CL
At high speed and low CL

explanation: The induced-drag difference between the wings is proportional to CL·ΔCL, largest at high CL.

question: Differential ailerons reduce adverse yaw by:

options.text: Deflecting the up-going aileron through a larger angle than the down-going one

explanation: The larger up-aileron adds profile drag on the descending wing, offsetting the induced-drag increase on the rising wing.

question: A Frise aileron reduces adverse yaw because:

options.text: When lowered, its nose adds drag on the rising wing
When raised, its nose protrudes below the wing into the airflow, adding drag on the descending wing

explanation: The offset hinge makes the up-going aileron's leading edge project into the high-pressure flow below the wing, producing drag on the down-going wing and yawing the nose into the turn.

question: The standard technique to counter adverse yaw on roll entry is:

options.text: Coordinated rudder in the direction of the roll

explanation: Rudder toward the turn cancels the yaw away from it, keeping the slip ball centred.

question: Aileron reversal at high speed occurs because:

options.text: The aileron's air load twists the flexible wing, changing its α so that the net rolling moment reverses

explanation: Down-aileron load, acting aft of the elastic axis, twists the leading edge down. Above the reversal speed the lift lost by wing twist exceeds the lift gained from camber.

question: Aileron reversal speed increases when:

options.text: Density decreases at the same TAS only

explanation: Reversal occurs at a dynamic pressure proportional to torsional stiffness. Stiffness ×1.44 → reversal EAS ×1.2.

question: Large transport aircraft lock out outboard ailerons at high speed and use inboard ailerons and spoilers because:

options.text: Outboard ailerons produce too little moment
Outboard ailerons are needed for flaps
Inboard ailerons have more adverse yaw
Outboard surfaces twist the flexible outer wing most, risking reduced effectiveness or reversal

explanation: Inboard surfaces act where the wing is stiffer; spoilers produce lift loss without a large twisting moment.

question: The effectiveness of a trailing-edge control on a flexible wing, as speed increases toward reversal speed:

options.text: Falls progressively to zero, then becomes negative

explanation: Wing twist opposing the control grows with q; effectiveness ratio decreases from 1 (rigid) through 0 at reversal.

question: An engine at 5 m from the centreline producing 120 kN fails. Rudder: fin area 20 m², arm 15 m, ΔCL at full deflection 1.25. The minimum EAS at which full rudder balances the yaw is closest to:
If the live engine's thrust increases by 21 %, the minimum control speed (full rudder) changes by:
Minimum control speed (as IAS) with increasing altitude for a normally aspirated engine:
explanation: Rudder moment at a given EAS is unchanged; the asymmetric thrust it must balance falls with density.

question: An aft CG raises minimum control speed because:

options.text: The rudder moment arm about the CG is shorter

explanation: N_rudder = F_fin·l_v. A shorter arm needs a larger fin force, hence a higher q.

question: A windmilling propeller on the failed engine raises minimum control speed because:

options.text: Its drag adds to the yawing moment toward the dead engine

explanation: The yawing moment is (T_live + D_dead)·y; feathering removes most of the dead-engine drag.

question: Banking a few degrees toward the live engine after an engine failure:

options.text: Has no effect on rudder required
Uses a weight component to balance the fin side force, reducing sideslip and the rudder required

explanation: With zero bank, the fin force needed to balance yaw also produces an unbalanced side force, forcing a sideslip. A small bank lets gravity supply the side force.

question: A rudder ratio changer or limiter at high speed:

options.text: Locks the rudder at low speed
Reduces the available rudder deflection to protect the fin from overload
Increases rudder deflection at high speed

explanation: Rudder side load ∝ q; full deflection at high speed would exceed fin structural limits.

question: In a crosswind landing with the wing-down (sideslip) technique:

options.text: Rudder aligns the fuselage with the runway and into-wind aileron holds the drift
Aileron aligns the fuselage and rudder holds the drift

explanation: Rudder yaws the nose to the runway heading; lowering the upwind wing produces a sideways lift component opposing the crosswind.

question: Rudder deflection in level flight produces, besides yaw:

options.text: A roll in the opposite direction only
A secondary roll in the same direction through sideslip

explanation: Yaw creates sideslip; through dihedral effect and the forward-moving wing's higher speed, the aircraft rolls toward the yaw.

question: Moving the elevator trailing edge up:

options.text: Decreases the download and pitches the nose down
Increases the tailplane download and pitches the nose up

explanation: Up-elevator adds negative camber to the tail, increasing its downward force, rotating the nose up.

question: The forward CG limit is often set by:

options.text: Elevator authority to flare or rotate at low speed in ground effect

explanation: A forward CG needs a larger tail download; near the ground, reduced downwash further reduces tail effectiveness. Full up-elevator must still achieve the landing attitude.

question: An all-moving tailplane (stabilator) compared with a fixed tailplane plus elevator:

options.text: Produces more pitch moment per degree, since the whole surface changes angle of attack

explanation: Rotating the entire surface gives the full lift slope per degree, instead of the reduced effectiveness τ of a trailing-edge elevator — used where tail power is critical, e.g. transonic flight.

question: Elevator deflection controls load factor in steady flight by:

options.text: Setting the wing angle of attack and hence CL at the current q

explanation: Elevator → pitching moment → α → CL → lift = n·W at constant speed.

question: Gap sealing between an elevator and tailplane improves control effectiveness because:

options.text: It prevents leakage from the high- to the low-pressure side, which would reduce the pressure difference

explanation: Flow through the gap equalises pressures near the hinge and reduces the effective camber change.

question: Elevons on a tailless aircraft combine:

options.text: Elevator and aileron functions: symmetric deflection for pitch, differential for roll

explanation: Both up → nose up; one up, one down → roll.

question: Ruddervators on a V-tail produce yaw by:

options.text: Differential deflection, and pitch by symmetric deflection

explanation: Each surface's force has vertical and lateral components; symmetric deflection sums the vertical parts, differential deflection sums the lateral parts.

question: Flaperons combine:
explanation: Both ailerons droop together for lift and deflect differentially for roll around that datum.

question: A taileron (differentially moving stabilator halves) is used to:

options.text: Provide roll control, typically at high speed where wing ailerons suffer aeroelastic losses

explanation: Differential stabilator deflection produces a rolling moment from the stiff tail, avoiding wing-twist losses.

question: Fully powered, irreversible flight controls require an artificial feel system because:

options.text: Aerodynamic hinge moments no longer reach the pilot, who could otherwise overstress the aircraft

explanation: Without feel, a small input produces large deflections at high q. q-feel scales stick force with dynamic pressure to restore natural cues.

question: A q-feel system makes stick force:

options.text: Increase with dynamic pressure for a given deflection

explanation: Force proportional to q mimics a reversible control and scales with the aircraft's response to deflection.

question: With irreversible powered controls, air loads on the surface:

options.text: Are fed back directly to the pilot
Cause the surface to float freely
Are reacted by the actuators and not fed back to the controls

explanation: The hydraulic actuator holds position; the pilot feels only the artificial feel unit.

question: Control harmony means:

options.text: Forces and responses in pitch, roll and yaw are proportioned so that coordinated inputs feel natural (typically roll lightest, yaw heaviest)
All three controls need equal force

explanation: Balanced gradients prevent over-controlling in one axis while another feels heavy.

question: At high speed, control-surface deflection to produce a given moment is small; the risk from large deflections is:

options.text: Structural overload from the high q

explanation: Moment and load ∝ q·δ; at high q, full deflection can exceed limit loads — hence deflection limiters and load-alleviation laws.

question: Steady roll rate at constant aileron deflection is limited by:

options.text: Roll damping from the wing's spanwise α distribution

explanation: Aileron moment = damping moment → p = constant. Damping ∝ q·(pb/2V), aileron moment ∝ q·δ.

question: Doubling the chord of a control surface (same span, deflection and C_h) changes the hinge moment by:
explanation: H = C_h·q·S_c·c_c with S_c = span × chord → ∝ chord². Hinge moments grow rapidly with surface size.

question: A servo-tab-controlled elevator at very low speed (taxi) is:

options.text: Largely ineffective, since the tab's aerodynamic force is too small to move the surface

explanation: The surface is moved only by tab lift ∝ q; at negligible q there is no force to deflect it.

question: The critical engine on a twin with both propellers turning clockwise (viewed from behind) is:

options.text: The left engine, since the right engine's descending blade acts further from the centreline

explanation: At high α the descending blade produces more thrust (asymmetric blade effect). On the right engine it lies further outboard, giving the larger yawing moment; losing the left engine leaves that larger moment.

question: Fin and rudder effectiveness at a given q is reduced in a large sideslip because:

options.text: The fin approaches its stalling angle and the fuselage may blanket it

explanation: Sideslip is the fin's angle of attack; near its stall its lift slope and rudder effectiveness fall. Dorsal fins delay fin stall.

question: The rolling moment produced by ailerons increases when the ailerons are placed further outboard because:

options.text: The local chord is larger outboard
The moment arm from the aircraft centreline is longer

explanation: Rolling moment = ΔL × spanwise arm; outboard placement maximises the arm (but increases aeroelastic twist).

question: Elevator effectiveness is reduced in ground effect mainly because:

options.text: Reduced downwash raises the tail's angle of attack, reducing the download and requiring more up-elevator for the same pitch

explanation: The tail sees less downwash; to produce the same nose-up moment the pilot must apply more up-elevator — the flare becomes limited at a forward CG.
